size.text: Once we know the size, we can estimate effort and duration. Size comes in two units: lines of code, a physical measure, and function points, a functional one.

loc.text: Lines of code depend on the language. To convert, use a gearing factor: the average lines of code per function point. In Java, one function point is about fifty-three lines.

cls.text: Then classify the project. Under five hundred function points: simple. Under a thousand: average. A thousand or more: complex.

rules.text: From function points, use the engineering rules. Duration equals F P to the power A. Staff equals F P over one hundred fifty. Effort equals staff times duration.

rulesEx.text: For five hundred function points, an average project, A is zero point four. Duration: about twelve months. Staff: three point three. Effort: about forty person-months.

cocomo.text: From lines of code, use COCOMO one. Effort equals a, times K LOC to the power b. Duration equals c, times effort to the power d. The idea: effort grows faster than size.

classes.text: Organic projects are small, with an experienced team. Semi-detached are medium, like a web app. Embedded are tied to hardware, like an antilock braking system.

cocomoEx.text: The same project is about twenty-two thousand lines. As semi-detached: effort, about ninety-seven person-months. Duration, about twelve months.

weighted.text: Two methods, two answers. The slide weights them seven to three: seven times forty, plus three times ninety-seven, over ten. About fifty-seven person-months.

units.text: Remember the units. Duration in months. Effort in person-months.
